name: Cicada 3301
title: A Plastic Duck Led Thousands Into the Strangest Job Test Online
claims: Cicada 3301 is the name given to three sets of puzzles posted online under "3301" between 2012 and 2014 | 1
The first puzzle started January 4, 2012, on 4chan and ran for nearly a month | 1
A second round began January 4, 2013; a third was posted on Twitter January 4, 2014 | 1
The third puzzle remains unsolved | 1
The stated intent was to recruit "intelligent individuals" | 1
A new clue was posted on Twitter on January 5, 2016 | 1
The last verified OpenPGP-signed message came in April 2017, denying the validity of any unsigned puzzle | 1
The puzzles focused on data security, cryptography, steganography and internet anonymity | 1
Called "the most elaborate and mysterious puzzle of the Internet age"; listed by The Washington Post as one of the top 5 eeriest unsolved mysteries of the Internet | 1
Speculation includes NSA, CIA, MI6, Mossad, a Masonic conspiracy, a cyber mercenary group | 1
Others say it is an alternate reality game, though no company or individual has tried to monetize it | 1
Theories include a secret society to improve cryptography, privacy and anonymity, or a cult or religion | 1
Several 2012 solvers said 3301 typically uses non-puzzle recruiting but made the puzzles to find members with cryptography and security skills | 1
A 2013 solver said solvers were asked about support of information freedom, online privacy and freedom, and rejection of censorship | 1
Satisfactory answerers were invited to a private forum and told to devise and complete a project furthering the group's ideals | 1
That solver did not finish work on a method of general decryption, and the website was removed | 1

Another 2013 winner documented her experience in a video series promising a more realistic, fact-based view; she facilitates a Discord community; other solver communities remain on message boards and forums | 1
Clues included images with hidden information, a telephone message, websites, and paper signs with QR codes | 1
Techniques included cryptography and steganography; references to literature, poetry, art and music | 1
Each clue was signed with the same OpenPGP private key | 1
Agrippa (a poem), Mabinogion (a poem) and The Book of the Law were used in the puzzle | 1
In 2012 Chile's Investigative Police (PDI) in Los Andes Province called it a hacker group engaged in illegal activities; Cicada issued a PGP-signed denial | 1

In July 2015 a group calling itself "3301" hacked Planned Parenthood's database; Cicada's signed statement said they were not associated with the group in any way nor condoned use of their name, number or symbolism; the hackers later confirmed no affiliation | 1
The US Navy released a cryptographic challenge based on the puzzles in 2014, called Project Architeuthis | 1
Person of Interest's 2015 episode "Nautilus" featured a similar worldwide cryptographic game with a nautilus shell; its creator said Cicada 3301 was the inspiration, with the quoted words | 1
2021 comedy-thriller Dark Web: Cicada 3301, directed by Alan Ritchson, follows a hacker in the recruitment game evading the NSA | 1

A 32-year-old cultural studies PhD working on a paper about institutional secrecy and the national security apparatus, in a Brooklyn studio, on a Friday at 10 p.m. in January, trains on the Williamsburg Bridge shook his desk | 2
He was scanning the /b/ board on 4chan | 2
4chan has no search function, no tagging, no registration, no formal archive; most posts expire or are deleted within hours; over a million posts a day | 2
LOLcats and Rickrolling originated on 4chan; 4chan helped spawn Anonymous | 2
Commenters suggested the message might be an NSA recruiting exercise; he had read the NSA was using 4chan to scout hackers | 2
About 40 commenters were discussing the image and many took it seriously | 2
Opening the image in WordPad revealed at the bottom: TIBERIVS CLAVDIVS CAESAR says "lxxt>33m2mqkyv2gsq3q=w]O2ntk" | 2
Tiberius Claudius was the fourth Roman emperor; shifting back four letters revealed a URL (Caesar cipher) | 2
The site showed a plastic duck and the text "WOOPS just decoys this way. Looks like you can't guess how to get the message out." | 2
Someone linked "guess" and "out" to OutGuess; running the image through it extracted a link to a subreddit | 2
The subreddit showed Mayan numerals, garbled letters, and two images labeled welcome and problems? | 2
Someone posted a link to an anonymous Mibbit chat room; he felt "a bit creepy"; he said most trolls don't put this much energy in | 2
He retreated to his bedroom and worked through book codes, King Arthur and the Holy Grail with index cards, uncovering "call us on us tele phone number..." | 2
He announced it in the chat; advanced commenters doubted, less advanced insulted; he received a private message "You're way ahead of the others" and an invitation to a private room | 2
The recording said "Very good. You have done well," that three primes were associated with the original image, 3301 one of them, to multiply them and add .com | 2
The first image's pixel dimensions were 509 and 503, both primes; the product led to a URL with a cicada image and a three-day countdown | 2
Hidden message: "You have done well to come this far. Patience is a virtue. Check back at 17:00 on Monday, 9 January 2012. UTC." | 2
It was 2 a.m. when he reached the next level | 2
The game was about to move from the web into real life | 2
